utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those listening to our procedures. Our apologies for the delayed start, due to some unforeseeable circumstances. The witness should be brought in. But to enable the witness to enter the courtroom, we have to go into private session for a quite short moment. Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony last Thursday still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, for the Prosecution, has more questions for you. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, and to everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Witness, the last question that I asked you on Thursday of last week was whether you remember the time in July of 1995 when Srebrenica fell, and you began to answer that there was talk about that; neighbours came to visit your parents; they would mention that Srebrenica had fallen. Can I ask you now to clarify whether any men who had fled from Srebrenica arrived in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in small groups. I don't know exactly how many they were, but I heard that some people had come through the woods. Yes, that's, more or less, it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please move closer to the microphone and speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, around that time in July of 1995, was there any shelling in Zepa that you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day, there was fire, and my mother mostly looked after me so that I don't go out and come to harm. I was in a shelter near our house and heard detonations daily. Well, it was an ugly experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember or have any impression of the intensity of the shelling on those days, how many shells were falling?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were maybe about -- well, because I counted, you know, when I was in the shelter, sometimes there would be five, sometimes one, sometimes two hundred and fifty, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was anyone in your village hurt in the shelling?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two persons who had left to fetch some food for lunch, but they weren't seriously injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who were those persons?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was younger and one was elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were they men or women?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Women.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did your family leave your village at some point in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, they didn't go anywhere. My mother was there, and my father too. He minded the livestock so that we wouldn't lose any, because that's how we basically made a living, and so we tried to keep them safe from the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you ever go up and seek refuge at any place outside of the village?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but only when we would go to the field and gather some food, such as potatoes or fruit and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And in that month, July of 1995, did you ever spend time in the meadow area at Zvijezda?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I don't know the exact date, but that territory of Zepa was supposed to -- or, was expected to fall. We left off with my sisters, my mother and father, to the Zvijezda Mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where did you stay up at the Zvijezda Mountain?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some summer cottages there, or weekend houses, if you will. We spent some time up there, maybe a week or two, but not more than that. I don't remember exactly how long we stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was there any shelling while you were up there?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Sometimes there was some shelling, but we were always able to find shelter. There wasn't so much, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you go somewhere after Zvijezda?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a courier came from down there and said to us that we should withdraw to the centre of Zepa, where the school is and a fountain. And we came down with my mother and sisters, and there were many people gathered there for deportation, I believe, in the direction of Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did your father come down to Zepa town?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he stayed up on the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know why he stayed away from the town?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably because he was a bit older, and he thought that where the others go, that he could go as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You said that there were many people gathered in the town in the area where there was the school and the fountain. Can you give us, as clear as you remember, your description of the scene that you saw down there concerning the people who were there, the atmosphere, please?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were mostly women, children. The atmosphere was, of course, very tense because we were all surrounded by the Serb soldiers, if I may call them that. And I stayed there with my mother and sisters, waiting to be put on a bus to be deported, but then those events happened. And one of the soldiers approached me, but I don't know his exact name, and he simply asked me, Where are you going, sir? And I said to him, I'm getting on the bus with my sisters and my mother to reach the free territory. And then he said to me, Wait a moment here, and move away from the bus. I didn't know why. I didn't know what he wanted. And then I thought to myself, Good God, maybe this is my last day of life, and I bid farewell to my mother and sisters and went back toward Zvijezda Mountain to find my father, which I did. I stayed there with him. I stayed maybe two or three days, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you recall what was the manner of the Serb soldier when he spoke to you? How did he speak to you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was very unpleasant, unkind. I probably looked older than my age, and maybe he thought that I was actually a soldier. And I said to him, Sir, I'm very young, I only turned 15 on the 15th of July. And he didn't believe me, I guess, and he said that I should step away from the bus and wait until he returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I extend my regards to all those present and wish peace unto this house, and may this day in court and the final judgement reflect God's will. On page 4, line 23, the witness did not mention to which forces the soldier belonged, he only mentioned a soldier, whereas Mr. -- but the Prosecutor asked him whether it was a Serb soldier. Actually, the Prosecutor put to the witness that it was a Serb soldier, whereas the witness didn't mention to which army that soldier belonged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, perhaps you didn't hear everything the witness said. He said: "There were mostly women and children. The atmosphere was, of course, very tense because we were all surrounded by the Serb soldiers, if I may call them that." That is exactly what the witness said, and Mr. Elderkin was just referring to this explanation by the witness. Mr. Elderkin, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, how did you feel when this Serb soldier addressed you in such a way?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was very uncomfortable. I thought that this would be the end of my life. I was only 15 years old, 15 years and 7 days, and I thought this is the end. And I decided to go away, not to wait for him until he returned. As I mentioned before, I bid farewell to my mother and sisters, and then went back to find my father and the other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you manage to find your father?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found him very soon, after some five or six hours, because that was how much I needed to get back there from the centre of town, because the terrain was very rough and steep.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And was he in the same area that you had left from with your mother and sisters?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, he was there. We had some land up there, my father owned it, and he was there with some men. I don't know exactly how many, but it was a significant group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that area with your father and these other men?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Maybe two or three days, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was there any shelling during that time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was frequent shelling, so that we kept in hiding to protect ourselves from the shells. We sought shelter behind trees so that nobody should come to harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: At some point, then, did you leave that area?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We went in the direction of Poljanice, I think the place is called. It's near Luke village. There was a meadow, quite a large one, and most men were gathered there. There was quite a large number of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know who had made the decision to move in that direction?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who exactly took that decision, but we were told to walk toward Luke village and, more specifically, the Poljanice meadow. There was a large number of men, and we spent the night there. Then we went down to the Drina. The name of the place was Crni Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was your father in the army or active in the defence of Zepa in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never saw him with weapons. He may have been, but he never told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And do you know if any of the other men in the group you were travelling with may have also been involved with the army or in the defence of Zepa in that year?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably, yes, but I didn't see anybody carrying arms in that group. Probably, the people around them were so as to keep that place, that meadow, safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were any of them wearing any kind of military uniform or clothing?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really didn't see anyone. They all wore civilian clothes. Maybe some of them did wear uniforms, I don't know, but I didn't really see anybody amongst us wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You said you went down to the Drina River at Crni Potok. How long did it take you to reach the river from the time you set off?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, two hours, maybe, because it's craggy and we also had to be very careful so that we don't hurt each other accidentally by maybe kicking a rock downhill or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And is that two hours the journey time from the meadows at Zvijezda or from the place where you grouped at Luke?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. From that place near Luke, we took two hours to descend, thereabouts, two hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And from Zvijezda to Luke, how much time was that journey?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we moved at night, and it took us five to six hours, at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: During this journey, was there any shelling?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but, fortunately, nobody was hurt. And it was night, too, so there was no visibility for them to target that specific location more accurately. All the shells fell rather close, but none actually hit the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you describe to us how the river and the landscape is at Crni Potok?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's very bad. The river is in a canyon, and when you're down there, you can only see the sky, nothing else, and, of course, the rocky walls. That's part of the river canyon. I don't know where exactly it leads, but it's very rough, and it's difficult to access it. And people would stumble and fall rather often, and then, of course, we would help each other out because there was no doctor or medical assistance. It was very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Why had you gone to this difficult place on the river, rather than to an easier location?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't because all the other places were probably - at least that's what I heard people say - exposed to sniper fire or shelling, so we found the canyon. We thought the canyon was the only route that we could take without anybody getting hurt by a shell. Probably, one of our men said that we had to go that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Once you got to the river, what happened?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first some people built a raft for us to be able to cross the river, because the distance was about 150 metres, I guess. This is only an estimate. And the water I was also deep at places. So we reached this spot by the river and moved on. Somebody would swim, others would get on the raft. But the raft was only big enough to carry five or six people, because we were all afraid that somebody might fall off and drown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And how did you get across the river?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I swam across, holding on to the raft. My father was on the raft because he couldn't swim, and I was there to help him, if necessary, either me help him or him help me. But most probably it would have been me helping him, because he couldn't swim, and I wanted to keep an eye on him at least as long as we don't reach the other bank, whereas for the remainder -- for the remainder of the time, it was mostly him who watched over me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And how long did it take to get across?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe some 15 minutes or so, because some people had already swam across and there was a string or a cable that they used. One group pulled the raft one way, and the others pulled it back. So the raft, when it was full, it would cross one way, and then they would pull the empty raft back to the bank where we had started off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And was there any shelling while you were crossing?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not until the evening or at around dusk: There was shelling, but not at the very location where we crossed, though. They probably couldn't target that place directly, although I'm not very familiar with that type of weaponry. In any case, there were shells falling around us at distances of 50 to 100 metres from the place where we crossed the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where did you go after you crossed the river?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards Serbia. I believe the location is called Jagostica. The terrain was also quite forbidding, and I heard some people from the group say that we were heading for the border between Serbia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you reach the border?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what happened when you got to the border?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were stopped by border guards, I believe, the military. I'm not sure what to call them. Military border guards. They awaited us there. They told us to come out, all of us, not to cause any problems, and to leave whatever items we had on the meadow. There was a school nearby, and that's where the meadow was in front of it. They searched us there. They were rather fair. They said if we had jewellery or money, to keep it with us, but that we should discard any sharp objects or weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The border guards who stopped you, which side of the border were they on, on the Bosnian side or the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Serbian side, that's where we were stopped by the border guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And how many people had crossed over at that location?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 480, although I'm not positive. I didn't write that down. So speaking from memory, I think there were some 480.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And among those people, were there any other boys of around your age?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, another two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know what year they were born?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were around my age, born in the 1980s, although I don't know when exactly they were born.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How about elderly people? Were there any old men in the group?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I remember that there were three old men of around 80 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Had they also come across the river at Crni Potok?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What happened after you had crossed the border and you said the guards searched you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were searched there. They checked us, and the father stayed by my side at all times, telling me that I shouldn't be afraid and that they wouldn't hurt us. They had some machine-guns, I think, in front of us, and again I thought I was counting my last moments and that I wouldn't leave that place. I believed we were all going to be killed there and then. Luckily enough, it didn't happen. Some military vehicles arrived. They put us on them, and we left, although I don't know where because by that time it became dark. We drove for a while, and all I know is that early in the morning, an officer who was there told us that we arrived in Uzice in Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you spend some time after that in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spent I don't know exactly how many, but around 20 days. From there, we were again deported to - what was it? - Mitrovo Polje, near Vrnjacka Banja and Prus, that was the name of the place, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, again, is Mitrovo Polje in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How were you accommodated?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some hangars or warehouses there. We spent two days in them, and then we were moved to two school buildings, where we stayed for a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were you ever registered by any official bodies; the Red Cross, for example?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, the Red Cross registered us, although I can't recall on what date. Perhaps a month and a half later is when they arrived. They took our particulars and asked us some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When did you finally leave Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In November 1995. No, I don't know exactly. In winter-time, in any case. I think it was in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that we were to go to a place in Vojvodina where a prison was. We waited there for two to three days, following which a group of us was deported, including myself, to Australia, and the other was sent to Europe and America.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And at some point, did you return from Australia to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. No one asked me, because my father was with me all along. If I had been of age, I could have decided to stay, but in this situation I simply had to go back with my parent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to show you a map now of the Zepa enclave and ask you to mark, for our information, some of the locations that you have described to us. Could we see, please, Exhibit P104 - that's the map book - and at page 13 in e-court. If we could ask for the Usher's assistance for the witness to mark the map, please. Sir, first of all, could I ask you to mark with a number 1 your village, Pripecak?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's here [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Then, please, could you mark the area of Zvijezda, where you fled when Zepa came under attack after the fall of Srebrenica, put a 2, please.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you then please show us the approximate route you followed to get to the Drina River? So after you had been to Zepa town and back again to Zvijezda, what route did you follow from Zvijezda towards the Drina?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And at the point where you crossed the Drina, could you please mark the figure 3?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, finally, if you could please continue the route to, roughly, the point at which you arrived at the border with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if you could mark the final point there with number 4.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Those are all the markings that I require. I would ask Your Honours if this marked exhibit could be entered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked map will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, marked map under Exhibit P104, map number 13, shall be assigned Exhibit P2189. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, thank you very much. Your Honours, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir -- first Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness. Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 4, line 10 of today's transcript, you stated that: "A courier came from down there and said to us that we should withdraw to the centre of Zepa, where the school is and the fountain." My question is: Who was this courier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know his name. This is what my father told me. I don't know his first and last name, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Do you know where he was from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Was he one of your people or from the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, he was one of our people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And one follow-up question by me. Did he wear a uniform, this courier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I didn't see him. My father wouldn't let me go out anywhere, so that no harm could come to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Sorry, just one more question. You stated that ultimately you left for Australia. Did your father come with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, now it is the turn of Mr. Tolimir to put questions to you during the cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to greet the witness and wish him a pleasant stay. May this hearing be concluded in keeping with God's will and not my own. I would like to greet everyone present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, tell us this, please: Why do you keep using the term "deportation," when you crossed over into Serbia voluntarily, where you also decided where to go onwards to Australia or America? Is this use of the term accidental or is there a purpose -- is there a reason why you use it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Someone decided, maybe from the ICRC, where the deportation would take place. As for when we went to Serbia, we were probably ordered by someone to do that. I really can't recall, though. I don't remember saying or having been said anything of the sort. I'm not ashamed to say what I know, but this is all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this group, including your father and you, know that Serbia provided its consent for you to cross over, and that is why the guards at the border did not open fire at you and you had no problems getting across?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. No one told me that. I don't know if it is so or not. There was no one who could tell me anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During your examination-in-chief, you said that you were ordered to go, and you repeated it a moment ago, you were ordered to go to the river, and then across, and then to America, Australia, and so on and so forth. Please tell us, since you were only 15 at the time, did your father and older people know that your crossing over the Drina was arranged with the authorities in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I had no occasion to hear that. No one told me anything of the sort, no one mentioned any agreement. I still don't know whether there was anything. I don't know if anyone said that, or if someone said that we had to go, or if there was an agreement or treaty that was signed. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that General Smith, as UNPROFOR commander, testified that following the London Conference, there were talks between international community representatives and Serbian authorities about your crossing over into the territory of Serbia from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I can specify the transcript page. Mr. Smith said, at page 11572, lines 12 and 13, I quote: "Speaking from memory, I believe I had proof that people crossed the Drina and entered Serbia at around that time." And here he means the time when you were there. Then, on page 11573, lines 11 and 12, he said: "I wasn't concerned at the time because I understood that there was a back door across the Drina to Serbia. That was the only way out for the remainder of military-abled men." Next, when I asked him in cross-examination at page 1168 [as interpreted] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That's what the accused said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "... I don't remember ever receiving any proof, such as a list of persons or similar. What I do believe or what I do recall is that I was told that some people crossed the Drina to go to Serbia." Then at page 11602, line 12, he said: "I know that Carl Bildt was in charge of the talks. I knew of it at the time. I knew that results were achieved and that it was possible for people to cross the Drina." He doesn't know who informed whom, but he also said that that information was limited, that talks were underway, and there was no other information that could be used at the time. Having in mind all of these things that Mr. Smith said, I want to ask you the following: A moment ago, you said you followed a canyon. Did you take the canyon to take shelter and covertly cross over into Serbia so as to remain unnoticed by the VRS in order to reach the location which had been arranged for you to cross over into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were simply taking cover because there was shelling. As I said, the shelling didn't last for long, though. We were simply looking for a shelter so that people wouldn't be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you put it that way, you also say that you were ordered to go. Do you know it for certain that there was an order for a secret passage to Serbia or were you free to go wherever you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that we were in a group. As for any orders, there may have been some, and you seem to say so, but I don't remember anyone ordering anything. You mentioned Carl Bildt and some arrangements. This may well be, but I'm not familiar with it. I didn't hear of such things from anyone. I don't know of any agreement with Serbia for us to be allowed to cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 11, line 3 today, you said: "We left all sharp objects, but we were allowed to keep our jewellery and money." Did anyone take any valuables from you while you were in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were others taken any valuable objects while they were in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot say either way. In any case, no one complained. We were still in a group, and I didn't hear anyone say that things were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you followed these proceedings, did you hear some of the witnesses who had crossed over to Serbia, that they were beaten, mistreated, and items seized from them?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. One morning, when I came out in front of the building where I was, I saw a man tied. We were just leaving for breakfast in a tent nearby. He was tied to a tree. I don't know why. I didn't know him, and I don't know who he is. I never saw him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you inquire with others what group he had come from and why he was tied to the tree? Was it because of his conduct or maybe because of his intentions?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't dare ask. I was afraid that the same would be done to me, although I was still a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 3 -- page 3 of today's examination-in-chief, line 2, you said that sometimes there were fire shells, sometimes one and at other times 250, and you said a result of that shelling was that only two women were wounded?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was a girl and the other was a woman. As for the shelling you referred to, it is true. In a minute or in a span of five minutes, I could hear 30 or 35 shells. We were simply in a shelter, and I couldn't go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Last week, on Thursday, on page 13221, the Prosecutor asked you whether you knew a "hodja," and you said you did. He asked you whether he attended any funerals, and you provided your answers. My question is this: Was there another "hodja" in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him, and my father used to say that he was the only one. Otherwise, I didn't have any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you referred to page 13221, but the transcript of that day didn't have so many pages. Please check the reference.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I referred to page 13231. It was page 76, line 21 then, when Mr. Elderkin asked whether the "hodja" performed any religious ceremonies and rites, and he had Hamdija in mind. At page 76, line 16, the witness said that his name was Hajric. I'm not sure I'm referring to the right pages, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, that can't be the right page. The transcript of last Thursday ended with page 13153 and 154. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do have a copy of the transcript that does, indeed, cover the subject of the "hodja" at 13231, so it seems that Mr. Tolimir does have the same source as I do. I would ask, though: Where is the reference to Hamdija? I didn't see anything or hear anything about anyone called Hamdija in the transcript last Thursday. But in terms of the page numbering, that's what I've got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have it now on the screen, and the page number is correct you gave us. In my document on my screen, I have a different numbering, but that might be a technical problem. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Elderkin. So I quoted page 13231, line 16. That's when Mr. Hajric said -- I may have misspoken and said Hamdija. The witness Hajric told us himself that his surname was Hajric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know who Mr. Hajric was?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I heard about this "hodja," but whether there was anybody else or something else, I really wouldn't know. I haven't seen it. I didn't have any contact with that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who was the president of the War Presidency in Zepa in 1995, in the time of the events that you testified about here?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Mr. Torlak, the president of the Executive Board of Zepa, on the 13th of August, 2010, in transcript 4543, lines 14 to 22, said: "As far as I know, Mr. Hajric was not a religious person in Zepa, he did not have a religious function. He was a 'hodja,' but he wasn't a religious leader. Before the war, he used to work in another village. There was a 'hodja' in Zepa. He remained there during the war, and he performed that function. As far as I know, he was 'hodja' in all Zepce ..." He's talking about Hajric here: "... and when the war broke out, he arrived in Zepa. In any case, he was not working as the 'hodja' of Zepa, because during the war it was another person who performed this function. This other person used to be in Zepa all the time, even before that. To put it simply, Hajric did not perform this function in Zepa." And then my question to Mr. Torlak: "Did you work as 'hodja' while you were the president of the War Presidency?" And he replied at 5444, lines 2 to 3: "No, never. That was his occupation, and he used to work as 'hodja' in a completely different place before 1992." My question: Do you allow for the possibility that maybe you don't remember the details about Hajric, about him being "hodja" and performing religious rites? Did you maybe confuse two different persons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying, once again, I don't know. That's what I heard. I heard there was a "hodja." Whether it was Hajric or Torlak, I don't know, I don't remember. I was a kid, and I was not allowed to go out. I couldn't go out and gather information. I really cannot remember. I didn't see those people. Maybe I just passed by, but I simply stayed for the most of the time close to my mother. I was not allowed to go far from the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you: Do you know a person with the name of Hamdija Torlak or did you know him at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we now have document P736. I'm going to ask questions about Mr. Torlak and Mr. Hajric on the basis of this document. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see here a decision by the War Presidency of Zepa. It says that all able-bodied men in Zvijezda, including you, should hand over their weapons. You can see the first line: "All able-bodied men from 18 to 55 years of age shall surrender their weapons ..." And so on and so forth, so that's their decision. And it's signed. You can see -- you can see the names that I'm asking you about: Mehmed Hajric, Hamdija Torlak, and Amir Imamovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just heard Mr. Tolimir refer to "all able-bodied men, including you." We've heard the witness's evidence. I don't believe it's disputed that he was a 15-year-old boy at the time, and I think that should be very clear on the record, rather than including him in the group of able-bodied men aged over 18 years of age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you help me? I don't see it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In that case, I -- it was something I heard. I also don't see it in the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then you should be satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. As long as it's clear on the record that it's not there. I believe it was said, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps, but it is not in the document. And, of course, I didn't hear it and we have it not on the transcript. Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Elderkin. I apologise for my mistake. I never said that this witness was able-bodied at the time. I said that he was 15 years old at the time. I'm showing him this document to see whether he can remember the names of the people who were the authorities in Zepa at the time when he was 15 years old. First, we see "Mehmed Hajric," who was the president of the War Presidency in Zepa. The second name is "Hamdija Torlak." He was a member of the War Presidency and the president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Zepa. The third name is "Amir Imamovic." He was a member of the War Presidency, and also he was in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, have you heard any of these names, and do you remember anything that you might have heard about them?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. I can't remember, no, which means that I don't know. I don't know anything about this Torlak, or Imamovic, or Hajric. I heard that there were some people like that, but I really didn't know who or what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise that I must have written it down incorrectly. On page 13297, that's what I wrote down: "Hajric was the only 'hodja' that I heard about, but I had no contacts with him. I met him only once or twice during the several years of war." That's what I wrote down, lines 23 to 25, transcript 3231, and I apologise if I didn't write it down correctly.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't write it down incorrectly, but I just can't remember this particular man. I don't remember his face. You know, it was five unfortunate years of war, and if you see this person once, this Hajric, I heard that he was a "hodja." Whether he was the only "hodja" or whether there was another "hodja," I really don't know. Maybe if there was some funerals, they would call a "hodja." Whether they would call Hajric or somebody else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now take a look at 1D738. That's a statement that you gave to the International Tribunal, ICTY. The statement is dated the 7th of November, 2008. And while we are waiting for this, I would like the first page not to be broadcast outside the courtroom. Can we go straight to the second page. Thank you. I'll repeat, once again for e-court, 1D738, 1D738.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That must be a mistake. Perhaps you're mixing it with another one. It's not to be found.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. Can we have 741, 1D741.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, there is no need to protect this document because the name of the witness is known, it's not under seal, and there's only face distortion, as we discussed last week. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement, page 2, the fourth paragraph, that's the large paragraph beginning with: "Sometime ...," you said that you remembered the day that you boarded the bus. And you said that the soldier approached you, that he asked you something, and after that you were afraid. That's what you said here. A soldier approached, asked you where you were going, and you got scared. My question is: Are you sure that it was a Serbian soldier who approached you, or was it maybe a soldier belonging to the BiH Army, the person who was doing the boarding of the buses?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been a Serb soldier. Even if there were some soldiers from our side, they were not able to come there and be on that location. It's logical that Serb soldiers and BH soldiers could not have been together at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived, how many people were there in the centre of Zepa, close to Fontana, and was it the first, the second, or the third day of boarding the buses?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the first day. I can't give you a precise number of people. There were too many of them. I can't give you a number. There were buses there, and there were many people around them; women, children, elderly people. I can't remember that. I didn't have time to count them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see Mehmed Hajric, the president of the War Presidency, close to the buses, or Mr. Kulovac? He was a doctor. You surely remember him. Did you maybe see Avdo Palic or anybody among the people who had some sort of official function in Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see anybody making lists of people who were leaving in the buses so that later on it would be possible to establish which people were supposed to arrive at the destination? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were probably some people like that, but I didn't look around. I think there was one of the nurses there, and they were probably making some sort of a list of people who were supposed to board the bus. I had gone towards a bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you were registered as a passenger of the buses going from Zepa to Kladanj? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. As soon as I arrived there and tried boarding the bus, there was a Serb soldier who asked me where I was going, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since we are about to take a break, I'm going to show you a film later so that you can see the whole atmosphere and try to remember the things that I want to ask you about. Thank you for all the answers that you have given so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Indeed, we need our first break, and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I was told by the court recorder that there is now a correction in the transcript in relation to one quotation about able-bodied men from 18 to 55 years. And, indeed, you are now recorded as having said, and I quote, myself, now: "It says that all able-bodied men in Zvijezda, including you, should hand over their weapons." Now there is these words "including you" included, but I think you apologised to refer to the witness as able-bodied man at that time. That resolves that problem. We have it now on the record. You should continue your cross-examination. Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise once more to the witness if I called him an able-bodied man. I know he was only 15 at the time. We can re-confirm by asking the question once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you 15 years old at the time when the able-bodied men were at the foot of the Zvijezda Mountain, and did you have weapons then? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't have any weapons, and the people around me didn't have any either. At least I didn't see any carrying weapons. Probably some of them keeping guard did have some weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Witness. Could this please be recorded in the transcript, that the witness said that he didn't have any weapons. And I agree that at that time, 15-year-olds were not given weapons. Could we now please see P740. It's a video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have used the OTP's statement of the witness, 1D741. Are you tendering it or not? But you should indicate what you want to do with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No, I'm not tendering it. I was only providing a reference to arrive at this video-clip and at the time when the people boarded the buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now we see that it says "25 July 1995," the first day of the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that you arrived on the first day and that you were registered, together with your sisters, by somebody. Tell us, were you registered by Serbs or Muslims, for us to know?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where was the registration conducted; in front of the buses or in offices?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. My sister went somewhere and returned soon. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask both speakers not to overlap, but to pause between question and answer and the next question, because it's very difficult for the interpreters to catch everything if you are exchanging your discussion very fast. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we now please see P740. That's a video-clip of the evacuation of the population from Zepa on 25 July 1995. We want to show the portion from 36:14 through 37:50. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop here. This is 43:36 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see three Serb soldiers in front of this house. Can you see them?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see that right to the left of them, there are other persons dressed in camouflage trousers and olive-drab shirts, wearing a blue cap and camouflage uniforms, who are not armed? Do you know to which army they belong or do you happen to know them?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could they be members of the VRS too?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Maybe yes, maybe no. And the blue caps were caps as worn by the UN; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember that soldier, nor do I remember these three.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Did any one of these three stop you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply can't remember their face.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's continue watching the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, we stopped at 36:43. It wasn't recorded or translated correctly. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us continue playing the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop here, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We stopped at -- we stopped at 36:49.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see this soldier, and is he a soldier of the VRS or a soldier of the ABiH? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I never met him, and I don't know him by face either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But can you tell anything by the insignia, the uniform, the weapons? Thank you. Here's my question: Would VRS soldiers come to Zepa unarmed on the 25th of July? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were probably armed. The one who stopped me was. This one, well, I can't see whether he has any weapons on him. He's carrying some bag, or a suitcase, or something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's continue playing the video-clip from 36:49 on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop here. We stopped the video-clip at 36:59.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know the man in uniform behind the blonde woman? We can only see his head now, but a moment ago we saw him better.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I really don't. I don't remember the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know Avdo Palic, the commander of the Zepa Brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have only heard of him, but I don't know his appearance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please play on the video from 36:59 onward. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop here. Thank you. We stopped at 37:13.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see these people carrying the lists, standing in front of the buses, and they are about to let the people board the buses according to the lists? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see him, really. And he has his back turned on us, and so I couldn't notice him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see what he is holding in his hand? Is that paper or something?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it looks like paper. Probably a list of names that he called out for people to board the buses, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's play on from 37:13. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you now recognise this man? Can you see his face? Do you recognise him? Thank you. That's the one who was holding those sheets of paper in his hand a moment ago, and now we can see him better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says that this is Mehmed Hajric, but I kind of remember, through a haze, having seen him. But it's been a long time, so I don't quite remember his face to be able to say, yes, that's Mehmed Hajric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time of the events in Zepa about which you're testifying, was he the president of the War Presidency of Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can only repeat my answer. I really don't know whether he was the president of that body.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's continue playing the video-clip from 37:30 onward. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stopped the video-clip at 37:51.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know these two men shaking hands, these two men in uniform? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other man is you, probably, because I'm looking at you now, but the other I really don't remember. Probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know the man with the beard, wearing a blue shirt and jeans? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's continue playing the video-clip from 37:51 onward. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us, having seen part of the video-clip now about boarding the buses in front of the fountain, did you see people standing in front of the buses and other people with lists, and were these people the representatives of the Zepa authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the last part of his question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really haven't seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't seen him either. It's the cameraman of Mr. Smith, because he demanded that this be recorded. Could we now see P740 from minutes -- from 59 minutes through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm a bit confused, because the last picture we saw and you made this comment about a man of Mr. Smith, I didn't see such a person on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The witness said that he didn't see the cameraman, and I said I didn't see him either. And Mr. Smith, in his testimony, said that he demanded that a cameraman go there and that he sent them to Zepa. Thank you. And I didn't see the cameraman in the video-clip either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please answer the following question: Did you subsequently get any information about whether anybody was taken off the buses? I mean, I'm referring to the inhabitants of Zepa who came to board the buses on the same day that you were there too.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I was there on that day, yes, with a crowd of people, and I was with my mother and sisters. I always reiterate that I was with them. And then this man approached me, that Serb soldier. He told me, Come here, and I had to because he was armed. And then he went off, I don't know exactly where, and before that he said, Wait for me here. And I repeat that I was scared, simply, and I thought if I waited for him to return, I would end up here somewhere, he would probably kill me. So I was scared, and I walked off. I said goodbye to my mother and sisters and went to the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you. I know, because you said so, but did you have information that on that day anybody was sent back from -- and denied boarding the buses, and did you have any reason to be scared? Of course, you were a 15-year-old boy, so you may have been scared, but did you have any concrete reason to be scared, any specific experience? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I was afraid for my life. I was afraid he would kill me or do something to me. And I don't remember that anybody was -- anybody else was there, because I went -- I walked through the crowd alone, and I didn't pay attention to anything except for trying to avoid him, not running into him again. And I then took the route toward the mountain, and I knew the path well because that was the path I was -- I took to go to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were afraid you would be killed, and you were lined up, the Serb soldiers on the other bank of the Drina River, once you had crossed the river, and that your father had told you not to be afraid and so on. Do you remember that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I remember. Probably he was comforting me, saying, Whatever happens, we're together. And he was always holding my hand or something like that, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As a boy, could you have felt fear of the situation, irrespective of whether there was any true reason for it or not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course there was constant fear. Now, you're there, and the next moment, you may be gone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us continue playing from 59:45 onwards.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stopped at 59:57.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you hear General Mladic say, Hamdija, there are able-bodied men here? If you were unable to hear, we can replay it.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I just did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's keep playing from 59:57, and perhaps we can turn the volume a bit more up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone was turned off. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you hear General Mladic say, I don't want someone else coming before me and I don't want to hear of another Zepa Brigade being formed?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear him say that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's keep playing from 1 minute -- actually, 1:00:14, and could we have even a better sound so that I don't need to repeat. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. I forgot again. Could we keep playing so that we can see General Mladic entering the buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should put questions to the witness. He's seen this, and we know that already; it is in evidence. Please carry on asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you later on hear from your mother or sisters if they had any problems en route from Kladanj -- from Zepa to Kladanj on those buses?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. They said everything was fine. This gentleman we see talking probably -- well, they didn't tell me there were any problems. They just told me they got through. When I returned from Australia, I went to Zenica, and I found my sisters there and my mother.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's keep playing so as to be able to see what General Mladic tells the able-bodied men who were on the buses. Let's continue playing from 57:16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have seen all that. Is it necessary to see this long sequence again? Do you know anything about this General Mladic talking to people in the bus, sir? I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as I was told about him by my mother and sisters. They said they didn't have any problems and that they did get on their bus. I don't know whether he got into every single one. In any case, that's what they told me when I returned to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm only concerned about this repetition. I know this is a very long sequence, and if you received an answer by the witness, you should carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We heard the witness's answer. He knows that General Mladic did not divert anyone or take anyone off the buses, although he knew there were able-bodied men there. We heard him say that before. In any case, let's look at D111, page 28, item 97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this list should not be broadcast, if I'm not mistaken, because it seems to be a list with several names on it. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. At page 36 of the transcript, line 22, you have stated as follows: "... I would end up here somewhere, he would probably kill me." My question is: Did you see anyone killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could the witness please look at item 97, although the last name is misspelled. Instead of "z," there is an "s," and instead of the last letter being "b," it is an "f."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it you, if you look at these particulars?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's probably me, but some letters were wrongly changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know the person at number 98, just following you, and was he with you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not. He was a neighbour, though. It says here he was a soldier, but I don't know whether he was. He may have been towards the end, since at the time he was 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We are no longer interested in the list. We just wanted to know whether you could identify yourself on the list and whether you were registered by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was registered by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the answers you provided, and thank you for coming to testify. May God bless you. I wish you a safe journey back, and may you have success in your trade, which is a difficult one. Your Honours, this is all that I require of this witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before I give the floor to Mr. Elderkin: Can you tell us, did your father go with you to Australia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And did you return together with him to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Elderkin, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I would ask if we could go back to the same exhibit that was just up on the screen, D111, and at the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, please look at the line numbered 95 and read the name there, "Salic, Osman Jusuf," with the date of 1948. Who is that, please?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And is there any listing for him as to his status as a soldier or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: NESIB SALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't have any other questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, the Chamber would like to thank you that you came here to The Hague and to help us to establish the facts. Thank you very much that you were able to assist us. Now you are free to return to your normal activities and travel back. Thank you again. We turn into closed session to enable the witness to leave the courtroom and to maintain the protective measures. Please stay there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if I might ask for a very brief break as an indulgence. It's simply that I'm handling both this witness and the one that follows, and I would appreciate both the chance to shake this witness's hand and say goodbye and also get my affairs in order before we start with Ms. Palic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many minutes do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Really, a couple. Two or three minutes would be plenty just to walk out and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time to have the second break already now? Then we could continue 20 minutes past 5.00, and then -- it would be too long a time. No, that is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If that would work with the interpreters, that would then flip our session so we'd have the longer one at the end. I'm in your hands as to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's the best way to have the second break now. We will resume 25 minutes past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, is the witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: She should be, Your Honour. Before she's brought in or while she's being brought in, I wanted to raise a brief preliminary matter which I've informed to the Chamber and also to the Defence, and it concerns Ms. Palic's health. It's nothing that should disrupt the trial, but she did have a heart attack late last year, and I discussed with her in proofing whether she might need to take any additional breaks. She said that she thought she would be fine, but it might happen that she would want to have a short break. And I wanted to alert the Trial Chamber to that so there are no surprises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much. The witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Elderkin, is there any problem to have it on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: As far as I understand, no, it's no problem at all. I also asked Ms. Palic whether she was happy to have that discussed publicly, and she said not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Palic. Welcome to the Tribunal. Please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. Please let the Trial Chamber know if you have any problems during your testimony. If you need a break at a certain time due to health problems, please just give us an indication that this is necessary. Thank you very much. Mr. Elderkin is now commencing his examination-in-chief and is putting questions to you. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, Ms. Palic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Please say your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: My name is Esma Palic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of March, 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And your religion?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: I was born in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Is that where you grew up?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: The first 15 years of my life, I lived in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And is it right that you went at one point to study at university in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I finished the secondary school in Rogatica and then left for my studies in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What did you study in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: First, I studied at the Electro-Technical Faculty, and later on I moved on to Psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: I am a psychologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When did you meet Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: We met in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was that when you were a student there?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Yes, during the studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did Avdo Palic become your husband?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In what year were you married?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: 1993, in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What was your husband's professional training?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: He was a mechanical engineer. That was his primary occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did your husband also complete his service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he served in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And after his initial JNA training, did he remain as a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he remained in the reserve as an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Are they boys or girls?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: I have two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When were they born, please?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: The older daughter was born on the 3rd of March, 1994, and the younger daughter was born on the 26th of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to go now to the year of 1992, please. Where were you living at the beginning of that year?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, I lived in Sarajevo. I had been living there for the past 10 years, in Sarajevo. On the 29th of March, 1992, I set out for Zepa. The 4th of April was Bajram, so I went to see my parents. That means that up until the 29th of March, I lived in Sarajevo. After that, I lived in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And when you went to visit your parents in Zepa for Bajram in 1992, did you plan to stay in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: No. I went to Zepa to spend a week there. As a matter of fact, I only took a few things with me in my hand luggage. And I suffered a lot during the war, especially at the beginning, because I had none of my personal belongings with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So your plan to stay for a week was changed. Why weren't you able to leave Zepa once you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: The reason was the beginning of the war on the Bajram, itself. There was bloodshed in Sarajevo. The first victim was killed. Zepa had already been encircled by the forces of Serbian Army. When I entered Zepa, the first night, from the surrounding hills around Zepa you could see tracer bullets coming and hear shooting. When I asked my mother what was it, she told me that the Serbian villages around Zepa had the situation for quite some time, it was a form of sowing fear among the population. And then it became clear to me why my father had advised me not to come to Zepa a few days before my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where did you stay exactly whilst you were in Zepa? Where was your parents' house?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
