utterances.text: The house of my parents is in the centre of Zepa, some 150 metres from the point of entrance to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did your husband come to Zepa for that Bajram with you?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Avdo worked in Vlasenica at the time. He was a teacher in a secondary school. He came to visit his father, but not for the Bajram. When the shooting started in Vlasenica on the day of Bajram, he and some friends of his managed to leave the town. Muslims were already being killed in that town at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: During the war, your husband served as a member of the Armija of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: By 1995, what was his rank?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: In 1995, Avdo was a colonel in the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And he was a colonel in what formation of the BiH Army, what brigade or unit?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: It was the East Bosnian Light Mountain Brigade or the brigade that was defending the territory of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of the population in Zepa during the war?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: During the war, there were only Muslims in Zepa, except two teachers, two female teachers. One of them is Jelenka Cesko. She was married to a local man. And the other one was Rosa Lazarevic. She had spent most of her career in Zepa, and she was a very dear neighbour of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did people move to Zepa from other areas during the war?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: During the first months of the war in 1992, and by that I mean April, May and June, there were numerous columns of people arriving in Zepa. Those were the people that had been expelled from the nearby towns and villages. The Yugoslav People's Army and the Serbian Army took over Visegrad, or, rather, the population who were non-Serbs, mostly the Muslims, who happened to be in Visegrad and who found themselves in the hands of Serbian soldiers were massacred. The inhabitants living in the nearby villages fled to Zepa, also the inhabitants of Rogatica and nearby villages, and the villages around Han Pijesak and Vlasenica, and at some point from Srebrenica as well, because at the very beginning of the war, Srebrenica was almost captured by the Serbian Army. It's a fact that Zepa was flooded by a huge number of people who had been expelled from nearby municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And why did they come specifically to Zepa rather than any other destination?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: I think that most of them ended up thinking that that was their misfortune. Some of them had family in Zepa. A large number of Muslim people thought that the war was not going to last long, that it was impossible for the war to last long, so they probably expected that the war was going to be over soon. That's one thing. They were also cut off. It wasn't possible to use other roads to come to some areas that were considered more safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you estimate the size of the population living in the Zepa enclave then, before the enclave fell in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: It's hard to estimate that. It was around 8.000. A large number of the newly-arrived inhabitants of Zepa was divided between Zepa and Srebrenica. A part of a family would live in Zepa and another part in Srebrenica. So the estimates are unreliable, but the number that was mentioned at the time was around 8.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask, please, now some questions about the shelling that took place in Zepa. Can you first tell us whether there was any shelling in the early years of the war when you were living in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: I have to say that there isn't a small town in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and probably not even in the world, that experienced greater suffering and was shelled with a wider variety of shells. Zepa was shelled by heavy artillery and also from aeroplanes. Also, during the time when Serbian forces managed to reach the high ground around Zepa, and when they had an overview over the whole of the territory, they also used PAMs and PATs, weapons using explosive charges, which led to my house being very damaged by that sort of bullets. They also used helicopters. In 1992, they used guided missiles for destroying the mosque in Zepa. They also destroyed several apartments in a building close to the mosque. They used incendiary devices, some kind of incendiary barrels that would then set fire to buildings. Also, they used those large bombs that were called "Hogs" by our people, although I don't know exactly what the name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You mentioned weapons called PAMs and PATs. If you're able to, could you explain what you understood what those abbreviations mean? What kind of weapons are those, please?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. These are the words that were used at the time: That's what we knew at the time. There were Pragas, there were PAMs, there were PATs. I'm not a soldier. I don't know exactly what it is, but we are talking about the ammunition that includes fragmentation bullets. Later on, we were bombed from aeroplanes as well. So it was hard to protect yourself from all this shelling. It was especially true for the first months of the war in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Specifically concerning the period up until May of 1993, where were the areas that were targeted with the weapons that you have described?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Well, there isn't a part of Zepa that was not shelled. There were some places that were shelled to a lesser degree. I lived in the centre, and I know that many, many shells fell there, both from aeroplanes and from tanks, but I can tell you that the same goes for other areas. Then the places in the Zepa municipality, such as Godjenje, Krivace and Stoborane, those places were captured in 1992, which means that the Serbian forces entered those places, destroyed everything, burned down everything, and expelled the population. The population fled for Zepa. So they used everything that they had. My husband was watching his house being destroyed by tank shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So were there occasions when your own house, your husband's house, was shelled in 1992 or 1993? And if there were, can you please tell us about those?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. I was mixing the interpretation and your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was your family house shelled in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Yes, my husband's house was destroyed in August 1992. It happened using tank shells. And then the house of my parents was shelled in December. One corner of the house was damaged. The glass was broken, and a part of the house could not be used for habitation. Then, in 1993, on the 8th of March, 1993, another shell landed and damaged the second floor. And that was probably the moment when I was closest to death during the war, because the shell literally opened a hole in the wall where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: During that incident or other incidents of shelling that you witnessed, were people injured or killed?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Of course, of course. Bearing in mind the number of shells that landed, we could say that there were few casualties. Whether that was due to self-discipline, I don't know. Most of the inhabitants spent their time, and especially the summer of 1993, in the caves. Zepa has peculiar features. There is a number of natural shelters among the rocks. And since the habit to seek shelter there remained from the Second World War, people did the same thing at the beginning of this war. However, still there were casualties, people were killed; my friends, my neighbours, the refugees, I mean, the people who had been expelled from their houses, from the places where they lived, and who arrived in Zepa only to be killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Among the casualties that you know of, did these include civilians, women, children, elderly people?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: I am now speaking primarily about that segment of the population; that is, the civilians, women, children, elderly men, people who were not fit for the military. The number of casualties among them was larger than the number of casualties among the military. There were not many deaths among the military in Zepa. When I say "not many," of course, every human life is a lot, but the fact is that Avdo protected people very much, and he was truly lucky in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In 1993, did the shelling decrease when Zepa became a safe area?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning, the UN entered Zepa and started to set up demarcation lines. And then there was some sporadic shootings, sporadic shells that landed on the demarcation lines, but it was definitely not as hellish as before, because before the UN came to Zepa, there was a large offensive by the Serbian Army in a village called Brezova Ravan, and they committed a massacre. That's a place on a hill from which you can see the whole of Zepa. And then later on, when the UN came, there was peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what was the situation with shelling in 1995? Could you please tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: In 1995, in the month of March, well, my memory is very good because that's when I gave birth to my younger daughter, and I remember perfectly many things. We called those shellings provocative shellings. They shelled the outskirts of town, and then they targeted areas closer to the centre. Avdo tried to intervene with UNPROFOR. However, those provocations, as we called them, continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could you take us through, then, after March, the successive months and tell us about the shelling, as best you can, say, starting with June of 1995, so before Srebrenica had fallen?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Some 10 days before the fall of Srebrenica, the shelling intensified. Shells fell closer to the centre, they fell in the centre and other inhabited areas. It was not as frequent as that, but the peace was gone. You couldn't be sure anymore that when you left your house, there wouldn't be a shell. And then it grew ever more intensive some 10 days or so before the fall of Srebrenica. And when Srebrenica fell, all hell broke loose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were there any casualties from this shelling?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Since I had a baby, and my other daughter was little more than a baby, I spent most of the time indoors in the shelter. But, yes, there were casualties from these early shellings. I know that there were casualties in the surrounding villages. But I especially remember a neighbour, an elderly man, who was killed by a shell, and I saw the body being carried away past the house of my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember whether that elderly man was a soldier at the time that he was killed?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: No. The man was killed in front of his door-step. He was not a soldier, he wasn't an able-bodied man. He was elderly. The shell killed him in his yard and not on the front-line. Well, there weren't any front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was your own house shelled during this period?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: My house was shelled when Srebrenica had fallen. But before that, there were shellings of other areas, but no shell hit the house directly. I was listening, though, when the Ukrainian commander, Dudnjik, told Avdo to remove his family from the house, because Kusic had asked him for the coordinates, and that the children and I were no longer safe there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You said that your house was, indeed, shelled after Srebrenica had fallen. Could you tell us, in as much detail as you remember, about that incident, starting with the date it took place, if you can remember that?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was on the 17th or 18th of July. Zepa had been shelled for days. We had been in shelters for days on end. People from Srebrenica had started arriving in Zepa, and they spread this terrible information. There were many wounded men there. They were in the shelter in the yard, whereas I, the babies, my mother and my sister spent most of the time in the house. It's hard to be in such a small space for a long time, and my younger daughter got nervous, so I took her to the living-room, where there was a little bit more space and more air, and I held her in my arms. But there was firing non-stop. My sister joined us and sat down. I was standing there with the baby. At that moment, a shell landed, and the front door of the house and the door to the living-room opened from the detonation. I ran back to the shelter, and so did my sister. The baby was crying. At that moment, the baby started vomiting, and I was really scared for her. Then we heard that a shell had hit a heap of firewood behind our house. Then there was another shell that hit the house, itself, and the third, and the fourth, and the fifth. There were five shells. And there were five of us in a very small and cramped space, and we were waiting what would be next. Then there was a lot of dust, and that was choking us. But the shelling stopped, and we knew that we had to escape. One reason was the dust that was choking us, and we were only waiting for that part of the house to be hit too. When I left the shelter, the house wasn't there anymore, we were outdoors, because the shells that had hit the house had pierced the walls and the roof. We were outdoors already. I remember that I had some milk in the hallway near the shelter, milk for the baby, but it was all dirty with plaster and -- well, it couldn't be used anymore. My sister ran out to the shelter in the yard, and I ran out with the other child, and then our mother followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, on that day, was your husband or anyone else from the army at the house or in the shelter with you when this shelling incident took place?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: No. Avdo was with the soldiers, and he heard the order being issued, Target the house of the boss's mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When you say he heard the order being issued, could you expand on that? How did he hear this?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but they were able to intercept the radio communication of the Serb Army. So they were up to date, they knew what the Serbs were up to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'll come back to your own sequence of events following that shelling incident, but on another subject: At around those days, did the Bosnian Serb Army address or broadcast to the population of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: We could hear them talking from the hills around Zepa using megaphones for days. I'm referring to Borovacke Stijene. That's the name of the hill. When I was in the shelter, I could only make out parts of those messages, but then on some occasions, I went outside to the balcony and I did hear that they were calling out to us to surrender. I'll never forget those words, because they coincided with my doubts and my darkest fears about my husband. The voice was calling out, People of Zepa, this is Ratko Mladic talking to you. And then something like, You cannot stay in Zepa. Take white flags and start walking toward Brezova Ravan, where there are buses waiting for you. Then you can be transferred to territory controlled by Alija Izetbegovic. Do not listen to crazy Avdo. You are his hostages. He will take you to death. The people were extremely upset then. The atmosphere that prevailed in Zepa, once Srebrenica had fallen, was -- can be described as a frenzy. The very fact that somebody's calling out to you not to listen to somebody you trust most confuses you even more, and I know that many were very upset when they heard that. People were running around. They even called at my house, asking, What shall we do, shall we surrender, and the like. They were coming to ask Avdo. And there was fear among the women, too. It was a situation that was making everybody crazy, and it was even intensified by these communications from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You said part of the message that you heard was something like, You cannot stay in Zepa. Did it surprise you? How did it affect you, to hear that specific message?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: I must admit that I was most upset by this message, Do not listen to crazy Avdo. You are his hostages. He will take you to death. And as for the message about the impossibility of staying in Zepa, we were very much aware of that. From the moment Srebrenica had fallen, we couldn't stand our ground there because in Srebrenica, there were far more UN troops. The surface area of Srebrenica was, more or less, the same as in Zepa, and they wanted to cleanse Zepa first back in 1992. And when Srebrenica fell, that automatically meant that Zepa would also fall. It was clear to us all those years that the Serb authorities and the Serb Army couldn't tolerate a territory -- or, rather, a place inhabited by Muslims so deep in the territory that they had cleansed, and there were repeated messages that we couldn't survive on the border with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You told us that the message you heard over the loud-speakers claimed to be Ratko Mladic speaking. Had your husband, at any point during the war, received any message directly from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was in 1993, when Zepa became a UN-protected zone, that's when Avdo received a message directly from Ratko Mladic. Ratko Mladic knew my husband before the war. He sent him a bottle of whiskey, I believe, and a packet of cigarettes, Drava cigarettes, and there was a short message on the wrapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 1716. And we also have the original of this document. I ask, please, for this to be shown to the witness, if necessary first to the Defence, although they had the opportunity and Mr. Gajic saw it just before we started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please, it should be given to the witness. Mr. Gajic, you and Mr. Tolimir know this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I had the opportunity to look at the documents during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, to continue, could you tell us: What is this document you have in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: This is the wrapping of that packet of cigarettes that Mladic had sent to my husband in 1993, and he had written this short message on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did your husband ever say anything about why Mladic had sent this gift to him? Did he ever explain his view as to why or what was the message that Mladic was trying to get across to him?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he told me. He told me that on several occasions, he had been offered to leave Zepa, because Mladic knew Avdo, and he knew that while Avdo was in Zepa, he wouldn't be able to enter easily, not only due to his military abilities or skills, because I must point out that Avdo had this influence on the population in Zepa that made them feel safe, they trusted him. So they offered him to leave Zepa and that they would reward him and enable him to settle wherever he wanted, but he refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask for this to be admitted as an exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1716 shall be assigned Exhibit P2190. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you also keep some other communications and provide those, a few years ago, to the Office of the Prosecutor here?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: When I was leaving Zepa, Avdo gave me a small folder, and I didn't open it for a long time. But then at one point in time, I opened it and found this cigarette wrapping, among other things. I also found letters exchanged between my husband and the wartime commander of the Serb Army from Rogatica, Rajko Kusic, or my husband and Dragomir Pecanac, who was a member of the Main Staff of Ratko Mladic and who, among others, was one of the key persons involved in the taking away and the disappearing of my husband once he was arrested in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You named Rajko Kusic as the commander from Rogatica. Was Rajko Kusic somebody who your husband knew personally?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: When my husband graduated from secondary school, he first worked for four years so that his younger sister could go to university, and he worked with Rajko Kusic. They worked at the filter factory. Before that, they had played football together. They were members of the Mladost Football Club from Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Please, could we see 65 ter 1717. And, again, I have the pack of original documents corresponding to that, and those are also offered to the Defence in the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please. But the last one, P2190, should be given back to the Prosecution, but we want to see it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I apologise for not having offered that up to the Bench first. The same for this packet, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To the Bench, please. The Chamber has seen this first document. It's given back to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Would Your Honours like to see the packet -- the second packet now or further wait until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, first use it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Very good, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If you look briefly at the packet of documents you have in hard copy in front of you, and tell us whether any of these documents were written by your husband.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: This is the first document which was written by my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And is that the document that is also appearing electronically on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if you could look through the contents of that document. And on the first -- either on the first page or through on to the second page, there are a list of numbered points, and if you could read through to those, please. On the English, they're on the first page of the translation, for the Court's information.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Well, if we look at this first page, it says -- should I just read out those numbered points?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: There's actually no need for you to read out loud the numbered points, except that I would like you to read the point numbered 1, please. That's the one which states: "Stop shelling Zepa every day."

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could you please tell us the date of this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is happening?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We need a doctor immediately, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, I hope this is not a big problem for you at the moment. We want to continue so that we can use the time for your interrogation, but we have to wait for a moment. If you need a break, please let us know, again. We have to wait for the Court Officer so that we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the moment, we can't do anything. Everything is arranged so that we can continue, and we should continue, for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, you have the floor, and I think there's no need to worry about the situation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Very good, Your Honour. We'll have to see how things develop.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, just to re-focus on the document in front of you, written by your husband, and we've just seen the numbered point 1. There is the statement: "Stop shelling Zepa every day." Could you tell us, please, what is the date of that document?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Avdo wrote the letter on the 18th of January, 1993, at 7.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, does this comment to stop shelling Zepa every day reflect the situation at that time, as you've described the shelling to us?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Before the UN forces arrived, Zepa was literally shelled daily, at daytime as well as at night-time, which was difficult to believe. There was no smaller place in the world that received more shells. It lasted until UNPROFOR came in May 1993. Zepa was not only shelled; the people of Zepa who happened to be there, and I feel the need to say that because I just read item 2, I wanted to say that the people of Zepa were literally starved. I said that the inhabitants of the surrounding villages and municipalities, when they fell in 1992 to the Bosnian Serbs or to the Serb Army, arrived in Zepa. Once they were there, the refugees outnumbered locals 3:1, and any food reserves went immediately. Luckily enough, it happened during the summer of that year, so people could try and come up with something. But if you will take my word for it, I didn't see a piece of bread for half a year. Larry Hollingworth, a humanitarian worker, tried to bring a UNHCR convoy to Zepa, and he took this letter to Kusic. He was persistent in his attempts to have the first humanitarian aid convoy reach Zepa, and it happened on this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. Could we now see the next of those documents, please, in e-court. The hard copy, I think, is the photocopied A-4-sized letter you have there, and in e-court that would be at page 5, I think, in the B/C/S and starting at page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Looking at this document, can you tell us, please, who is it from and who is it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: This is Rajko Kusic's letter to my husband. Since Rajko Kusic did not indicate a date, I see that my husband noted it down as March 1993; the 1st of March, I believe, of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And I'd like to go through some of the statements made in this letter. I'll read them out from the translation I have, and if you need time to find them in the original, then please let me know. So: "You cannot stay on the border to Serbia to separate us from our people. Go with your people to the place you belong to in Central Bosnia while there is still time. Europe does not allow Islam to go on. Don't you see that?" How do these statements correspond with your understanding of the objectives of the Bosnian Serb side in the war?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: This is definitely the prevailing opinion among Bosnian Serbs. Rajko Kusic simply put it on paper to convey it in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it possible that we have the B/C/S version not on the screen, that we should move to the next page? Thank you. I think there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'll just leave that up for a moment so the Defence have a chance to read through before I move to the next of these letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could we then go, please, to the document which is starting at page 9 in the B/C/S in e-court and starting at page 5 in the English. And this should be, in the hard copy, a document dated the 22nd of March of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, Ms. Palic, for your information, to confirm you're looking at the right copy, on the paper, that's the page with the stamp at the top left-hand corner of 0602-4475. Who is this document sent to, and can you tell us who is it written by?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: This is another letter sent by Rajko Kusic to my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And is it signed at the end, or how are you able to establish that it's from Rajko Kusic?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: My husband showed it to me. It is not difficult to compare the two handwritings with the previous letter, and it is the same. As for the contents, I can also conclude that it was written by Rajko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The first two of those letters we saw, written first by your husband and then by Rajko Kusic, were from 1993. We're now looking at a letter from March of 1995. I'd ask you again to scan through that letter, and towards the end there is a statement: "We are beginning to destroy your Turkey, and we'll get Zepa back and convert to Christianity, and we won't kill everyone." And that's seen at the bottom of the English translation and the last four lines of the bottom of the right-hand side of our screens. Did you learn, at the time of March of 1995, that your husband had received such a letter from Rajko Kusic?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Avdo showed this letter to me, and he just laughed. He was an incorrigible optimist, believing firmly that people would one day be ashamed of what they were doing at the time. This is how I remember him. For me, it wouldn't be simple to deal with if someone tried to communicate in this manner with me. It would be difficult for me to remain an optimist. He did, however, and he truly believed that people would repent some day and that everyone should use their own head to think carefully about what they were doing. He kept telling me that I was wrong, and this letter is yet another thing we discussed among us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask for this set of documents to be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 65 ter 1717 will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1717 shall be assigned Exhibit P2191. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if you'd like to see the pack of letters in the originals, we can hand those now up to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, we would appreciate it. We'll take it that the Defence had the opportunity to see it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't know that Mr. Gajic needs to confirm, but, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, you spoke earlier of refugees who had come to Zepa after the fall of Srebrenica. What, if anything, did you learn from those people about what had happened in and around Srebrenica after the fall?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Given that the men who arrived in Zepa were mostly wounded, they were placed in the hospital or in some of the houses. A number of them were also accommodated in my parents' house. The first one who came had his head and arm bandaged, since he had been wounded. It turned out to be an acquaintance -- a friend, actually, of my husband's whom I liked as well. At first, I didn't recognise him when he showed up at the door. I will never forget what he said once he was seated. He said, Avdo, I had to walk over my father's dead body. I did not even have time to bury him. He told us how they set out, trying to reach the free territory around Tuzla. He told about how the Serb Army intercepted them, cut the column in several pieces, how they mingled with them and killed them, how they arrested them. It was a terrifying story. Everything those people had to say made you wish that you weren't there. That was -- that seemed to be the only solution. The only other one was to fall in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about men being taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: As I said, the person who told us all that also told us that they went into the group, and since there was a lot of panic, they couldn't make out who was who. That was one thing. Another thing was that they kept intercepting them, setting up ambushes, and taking them away. Some were killed on the spot. They were being killed as part of the column in the forest. And this friend of ours managed to, at some point, turn back and go to Zepa to escape that. In doing so, he was unable to bury his father's body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to return to the day when your house was shelled, and you told us that was the 17th or 18th of July of 1995. Did you stay in the house after that day?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: No. The house had gone. We managed to reach the shelter in the yard. Once it became dark, my husband arrived. He suggested that we should all move, and we went to Stitkov Dol, which was some half an hour away from Zepa, on foot. He saw me there with the children, accompanied by all the people who were accommodated with us as well as the rest of the people from the settlement, itself. In moments of panic, almost as a rule, people followed Avdo's family, believing it would make them safer. It was in this same fashion that the people of the surrounding villages left with us, at the same time. And it was only normal, because by that time it was unbearable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know why your husband proposed specifically to go to Stitkov Dol?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: Stitkov Dol was closer to the centre and yet relatively safe or safer than other places. When I tried to analyse the situation, all of our moves in 1992 and 1993, as well as in 1995, were in that one direction. We, from the centre of Zepa, and the villages on the left-hand side, like Vrelo and Stop Polje and the others, all moved towards Stitkov Dol and from there to the Zepa Mountain. In 1992, the idea was to go from there towards Srebrenica because, in a way, it was en route to Tuzla. That was the idea that we considered and intimately called the Salvation Road. In 1993, as well as 1995, during the critical times when Zepa was under attack, I spent some time in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did people come from other areas of the Zepa enclave to Stitkov Dol or just from the group of villages you described close to Zepa town?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC
utterances.text: It is not a large village, and not everyone could come there. There were other safe areas or oases of peace, so to speak, where people went to. Some people had already gone to the Zepa Mountain before, so, in other words, not everyone was in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm watching the time on the transcript. It would be a convenient place in my list of questions to stop, unless Your Honours would prefer to continue for a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's a good idea to adjourn now. Thank you very much. We have reached the time for the end of the hearing for today. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom for the continuation of your interrogation. Thank you very much. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
